evidence: App.tsx: 50 hardcoded hex colors used as Tailwind arbitrary values (text-[#2d8c47], bg-[#e54833]) while the scene.color field already partially drives colors, creating an inconsistent color strategy

App.tsx contains Card (helper), Hero (independent component with state/effects), and App in a single file — three React components with distinct responsibilities

design_coherence.dimension_character: The codebase has solid foundational patterns — cva-driven button variants, CSS theme tokens, and a clean project skeleton — but App.tsx (85% of production code) accumulates multiple concerns that blur module boundaries. The scenes data couples presentation with content, color strategy is split between data-driven and hardcoded arbitrary values, and three component definitions in one file erode separation of responsibilities. A new team member would grasp the small components quickly but would need to untangle App.tsx to understand the boundaries.
design_coherence.score_rationale: The button and utility code are well-structured examples of earned abstraction, and the CSS theme system is a strong positive. However, App.tsx's mixing of data, presentation, and component definitions across 407 LOC reduces design coherence below what the otherwise clean patterns would suggest. Score 72.0 reflects adequate structural design with clear improvement opportunities that would benefit a new team member's onboarding.

App.tsx line 55: content text color hardcoded as text-[#2d8c47] instead of deriving from scene.color

Replace Tailwind arbitrary values like text-[#2d8c47] with references to the scene data or semantic tokens.

issues.summary: Scene data structure embeds full JSX in leftPanel, rightPanel, and content fields, mixing data with presentation

A developer adding a new scene must copy-paste the same JSX structure with only text/color diffs
issues.suggestion: Extract scene panel rendering into a data-driven approach: define scene data as plain objects (title, subtitle, color, cards: [{value, label}]), then render cards from that data with a shared SceneCardList component. This separates data from presentation and reduces the scenes array to ~60 lines of pure config.

issues.summary: Three near-identical scene panel render loops for left, center, and right panels in App.tsx
evidence: App.tsx lines 318-336: left panel renders scenes.map() with absolute-positioned divs, opacity/transform transitions, pointerEvents logic, scroll-down animation mask
App.tsx lines 339-364: center panel renders scenes.map() with same absolute-positioned divs, opacity/transform transitions, pointerEvents logic, different text layout
App.tsx lines 367-386: right panel renders scenes.map() with same absolute-positioned divs, opacity/transform transitions, pointerEvents logic, scroll-up animation mask

Each block differs only in content slot (leftPanel/rightPanel/content), scroll animation class (scroll-down/none/scroll-up), and transform direction (translateY(0.75rem)/translateY(1rem)/translateY(-0.75rem))
issues.suggestion: Extract a reusable ScenePanel component accepting props: contentSlot, scrollDirection, and translateOffset. The three render blocks would reduce to three <ScenePanel> invocations, eliminating ~60 lines of duplicated map/wrapper/transition boilerplate.

issues.summary: Three React components (Card, Hero, App) with distinct responsibilities defined in a single file
evidence: App.tsx lines 17-26: Card component — small presentational helper, but defined inside App.tsx rather than components/

App.tsx lines 214-262: Hero component — independent landing section with its own useState (showScrollBtn) and useEffect (delayed timer for scroll button), distinct responsibility from the scene carousel
App.tsx lines 264-405: App component — manages scroll progress, active index, renders Hero + scene carousel + footer
Hero has separate state lifecycle and could be independently tested if extracted
issues.suggestion: Extract Hero to src/components/hero.tsx and Card to src/components/ui/card.tsx. This makes module scopes explicit: App owns scroll orchestration, Hero owns the landing section, Card is a reusable presentational component. A new team member can navigate by file name rather than scanning 407 LOC.

root_causes: Rapid prototyping pattern where all code was written in a single component before extraction was considered
Scene data grew organically from a small array to 185 lines of embedded JSX without refactoring the structure
Color strategy evolved without a centralized decision — some colors were parameterized via scene.color, others were added as arbitrary values for quick visual tuning
possible_false_positives: Co-locating Card in App.tsx could be defended as close-to-use for a simple 8-line component; the real concern is Hero which has its own state

add.header: Button component uses cva for clean variants
add.description: button.tsx uses class-variance-authority to define a single buttonVariants call with variant/size axes. This is a positive pattern — variant definitions are discoverable, types are inferred, and JSX stays clean. A new team member can understand all button styles in one place.

add.header: CSS theme tokens via custom properties
add.description: index.css defines --background, --main, --border, --shadow, --radius-base, and spacing tokens as CSS custom properties with dark mode overrides. This creates a centralized visual design system that all components reference, preventing color/sizing drift across the codebase.

The scenes array mixes data definition (strings, IDs) with full JSX markup (Card calls, layout divs) across 185 lines in the same file as the scroll orchestration logic and three component definitions. This is the primary design coherence concern — a new team member needs to mentally separate data, presentation, and behavior within a single 407-LOC file.

scene.color drives subtitle badge backgrounds but content text and hero accents use hardcoded Tailwind arbitrary values. This halfway data-driven approach adds cognitive overhead — a developer must check whether a color comes from data or is hardcoded. Complete the migration to data-driven or centralized tokens.
